text: Linearisability is essentially the illusion of a single copy of data. We build distributed systems hoping to maintain that illusion, but physics and the speed of light violently disagree.
context: Linearisability is the gold standard for concurrent object correctness: every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its invocation and completion, consistent with a sequential history. The CAP theorem formalises a fundamental tradeoff: under network partition, a distributed system cannot simultaneously be consistent and available. Weaker consistency models—eventual consistency, causal consistency, session guarantees—each relax linearisability in different ways to recover availability or performance, but none can be composed with the same algebraic simplicity as sequential code. The unresolved tension is that most distributed systems documentation describes which model is used, but not the class of application-level bugs that become possible when programmers assume a stronger model than the system provides.

text: The kernel boundary used to be sacred. Now, if you want sub-microsecond latency, the first thing you do is figure out how to completely bypass it.
context: Kernel bypass networking (DPDK, RDMA) relocates packet processing entirely into userspace, eliminating syscall overhead and achieving sub-microsecond latencies that the kernel network stack cannot approach—but at the cost of abandoning the OS abstractions that provide isolation, fairness, and security. eBPF inverts this: rather than moving work out of the kernel, it allows verified programs to run inside the kernel in response to events, turning the kernel into a programmable substrate without requiring a module or a reboot. Memory-mapped I/O tunnels hardware register space directly into process address space, collapsing the device driver abstraction. The unresolved question at this stage is what the kernel boundary is *for*, now that the mechanisms for bypassing, extending, and dissolving it are mature: the remaining constraints are not technical but conceptual, about what invariants the OS is still responsible for maintaining when half the interesting work happens outside its control.

The unresolved question at this stage is what the kernel boundary is *for*, now that the mechanisms for bypassing, extending, and dissolving it are mature: the remaining constraints are not technical but conceptual, about what invariants the OS is still responsible for maintaining when half the interesting work happens outside its control.

text: The fundamental question of modern architecture isn't where to put the boundary, but whether a static kernel boundary makes sense at all. Fast paths are now application-defined.
